summary: Documents a common way for an agent supporting both SNMPv1 and SNMPv2 to map an SNMPv2 response into an SNMPv1 response. It was replaced by RFC 2576.

plainLanguage.summary: A translator turns messages written in the newer language into the older one so both kinds of machine can understand.

questions: how do snmpv1 and snmpv2 interoperate
subtitle: Translating messages between two versions of the network management protocol.

tldr.problem: Networks needed agents that supported both SNMPv1 and SNMPv2, but the two versions have incompatible error codes, exceptions, and data types that could not be directly translated.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2089 defines a standard mapping that converts SNMPv2 responses (error codes, exceptions, and types like Counter64) into SNMPv1 equivalents so that SNMPv1 managers can work with SNMPv2-based agents.
tldr.outcome: This mapping allowed the same agent to serve both SNMPv1 and SNMPv2 clients without reimplementing the core logic, easing the transition to SNMPv2. It was replaced by RFC 2576, which covered the full coexistence framework.

today: RFC 2089 is an Informational RFC and has been obsoleted by RFC 2576, which covers the full coexistence framework for SNMPv1, SNMPv2, and SNMPv3. However, the mapping rules documented here remain the standard way bilingual agents perform this translation.

sections.title: The Problem: Supporting Two Versions
sections.content:
SNMPv1 was the established standard, and SNMPv2 added new features and better error reporting. Many agents were built to support the new SNMPv2 underneath, but some clients still used SNMPv1. The core challenge: the two versions have fundamentally different ways of reporting errors and representing data.

RFC 2089 documents a standard way for bilingual agents (those supporting both versions) to translate SNMPv2 responses into SNMPv1 responses on the fly. This lets a single agent serve both old and new clients without maintaining two separate code paths.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a store that receives orders in two different languages from customers. Rather than having staff who speak both, they have a translator who converts everything to one language. That translator is RFC 2089.

sections.title: Mapping Error Codes
sections.content:
SNMPv2 defines many error codes: wrongValue, wrongEncoding, noAccess, notWritable, and others that provide specific feedback about what failed. SNMPv1 has only six error codes: noError, tooBig, noSuchName, badValue, readOnly, and genErr.

The mapping groups SNMPv2 errors into the closest SNMPv1 equivalent. For example, wrongValue, wrongEncoding, wrongType, and wrongLength all map to SNMPv1's badValue. Access-related errors like noAccess and notWritable map to noSuchName. This lets old clients understand what went wrong, even if they do not see the full detail.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like translating detailed error messages into simpler ones: 'the password is too short' becomes just 'bad value.'

sections.title: Handling Exceptions and Missing Data
sections.content:
SNMPv2 introduced exception values: noSuchObject, noSuchInstance, and endOfMibView. These let an SNMPv2 response say 'variables 1, 3, and 5 exist, but variables 2 and 4 do not' while still returning the ones that do exist.

SNMPv1 cannot return partial results; it either succeeds completely or fails completely. When an SNMPv1 request encounters an SNMPv2 exception, the agent sets the error code to noSuchName and tells the client which variable caused the problem by index. The varBindList is returned as it was in the request, unchanged. This ensures SNMPv1 clients see a consistent contract: either all variables succeeded, or one failed.
sections.plainLanguage: When a store finds that it has some items but not others, SNMPv1 customers get told 'sorry, we are out' rather than 'we have these three but not those two.'

sections.title: The Counter64 Problem
sections.content:
SNMPv2 introduced Counter64, a 64-bit counter for objects that increment beyond the 32-bit limit of SNMPv1's Counter. SNMPv1 clients have no way to parse a 64-bit value.

The RFC takes a simple approach: an SNMPv1 client must never see a Counter64 value. On a GET request for a Counter64 object from an SNMPv1 client, the agent returns noSuchName. On a GETNEXT request (which walks the tree), the agent skips the Counter64 object and returns the next one that fits SNMPv1. For traps sent to SNMPv1 managers, Counter64 varBinds are removed before transmission. This way, SNMPv1 clients perceive Counter64 objects as if they do not exist.
sections.plainLanguage: If a library system can only handle book numbers up to 999,999 but some new books have higher numbers, the system acts as if those books do not exist.

sections.title: Request Processing Steps
sections.content:
For an SNMPv1 GET request, the agent first processes it against the SNMPv2 instrumentation code and gets back SNMPv2 responses. Then it checks: is the error-status anything other than success? If so, translate the error code and return. If success, scan the varBinds for exceptions or Counter64 values. If found, translate the first one to noSuchName and return. Otherwise, return the data as-is.

For GETNEXT, the process is similar, but with an extra step: before checking for exceptions, the agent skips any Counter64 values and tries the next object in the MIB tree. This ensures the client always walks a consistent tree that excludes Counter64 objects.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a checklist: did the request work? If not, translate the error. If yes, look for values the old client cannot understand and hide them.

sections.title: Converting Traps
sections.content:
SNMPv2 traps (Inform messages) have a different structure from SNMPv1 traps. SNMPv2 includes three special variables: sysUpTime.0 (a timestamp), snmpTrapOID.0 (what kind of event), and optionally snmpTrapEnterprise.0 (who sent it). SNMPv1 traps use separate fields instead.

When sending an SNMPv2 trap to an SNMPv1 manager, the agent removes Counter64 varBinds and the three special variables. It then uses the trap type in snmpTrapOID.0 to set the SNMPv1 trap's generic-trap and specific-trap fields, and copies sysUpTime.0 into the timestamp. The remaining varBinds are sent as payload. This preserves the information the SNMPv1 client needs while dropping what it cannot understand.
sections.plainLanguage: Converting a new-style alarm to an old-style one: take the useful information, drop the parts the old system cannot read, and format it the way the old system expects.
